fixes.explanation: Jesus saw Levi, a tax collector, sitting at the tax booth. He told him, "Follow Me." Just two words. Short enough to fit on a sticky note.

I can see why you'd think that, since Levi was a tax collector. But the text has Jesus say something much shorter. He tells Levi, "Follow Me," and that's what He says to him. Nothing about repaying is in these verses.
Not this one, friend. Here, Jesus sees Levi at the tax booth and says, "Follow Me." That's all the text gives us for what Jesus says to him. Short and simple, like a note on the fridge.

Luke says Levi "…got up, left everything, and followed Him." Jesus told him to follow, and Levi got up. The text says he left everything, and I'd have a hard time leaving a counter full of warm dough.

Luke says "A large crowd of tax collectors was there…" Levi himself was a tax collector. So this was a banquet at a tax collector's house with a large crowd of tax collectors. Bring your own coworkers to the party and you get the same crowd.
Fishermen are a fair guess, but the text says a large crowd of tax collectors was there. Nobody mentions a single fishing net at that table. The others eating with them aren't named either.
Soldiers are a fair guess, but they're not named here. Levi's banquet had "A large crowd of tax collectors…" along with others who were eating with them. The text doesn't say who those others were.

Close, but the text adds a little more. A large crowd of tax collectors was there, "…along with others who were eating with them." So the guest list had more than tax collectors. That's why this one is false.
Healing isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses, so that's not the complaint. Here the question is about the table. They ask, "Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?"

Sacrifices don't come up anywhere in these verses, friend. The complaint is about who's sitting at the table. The Pharisees and their scribes ask, "Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?" They're watching that guest list like a hawk.

Jesus flips it around. He says, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick." So saying the healthy need a doctor is the opposite of what He said. He's answering the complaint about who He eats with.
Right. Jesus says, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick." It's the sick who need a doctor. And He's answering the complaint about who He's eating with.
I can see why that word came to mind. But Jesus says He has come to call sinners "to repentance." Judgment isn't the word He uses in this verse.

Service is a fair guess, but it isn't the word Jesus picks. He says, "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance." The call ends at repentance, and it goes to sinners, the very word the Pharisees used in their complaint.

The Pharisees and scribes say, "John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees frequently fast and pray, but Yours keep on eating and drinking." They're comparing the groups side by side, like a stats chart at the break room. Fasting and praying on one side, eating and drinking on the other.
Healing isn't in their complaint. They say Jesus' disciples "…keep on eating and drinking." It's all about the table again.

Leave is an understandable guess, but Jesus isn't talking about leaving yet. He asks, "Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?" The bridegroom is with the guests right now. Being taken from them comes up in the very next verse.

Jesus says, "…the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast." The words are plain, and I think they're a heavy thing to hear. He says it right in the middle of an answer about a wedding.

Jesus says, "…the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast." That's what the text says, word for word, so this one is true. It's a heavy line, and I think it deserves a pause.

Jesus says, "…the new wine will burst the skins, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined." Wineskins were containers for wine. Old skins and new wine don't mix, and Jesus says the skins are ruined and the wine spills.

That would be a happy ending, but it's not the one Jesus gives. He says, "…the new wine will burst the skins, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined." In His picture the skins don't hold it. They burst.
Jesus says, "…new wine is poured into new wineskins." New goes with new. That's the way around the problem He just described. Even I'd rather put fresh dough in a fresh bowl.
Jesus says "…no one after drinking old wine wants new…" So the person who has been drinking old wine doesn't want the new. In his words, "The old is better." That makes the statement true, not false.
